article.headline: Applied Optoelectronics Rides the AI Optical Interconnect Wave
article.lede: A post from @BlackPantherCap makes a bull case for Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI) following its Q1 2026 earnings: $151.1 million in revenue, up 51% year-on-year, with data-centre sales nearly tripling to $81.4 million. The underlying thesis is that Nvidia's Blackwell generation of AI accelerators is so much more powerful than its predecessors that chip-to-chip bandwidth demands will force a wholesale shift from copper to optical and photonic interconnects — and that AAOI is positioned to capture that spending. A price target of $400 by end-2027 implies roughly a 3× gain from the recent all-time high of about $192.
article.body:
Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI) makes the *optical transceivers* — modules that convert electrical signals to pulses of light for travel over fibre — that stitch together servers across data-centre switching fabrics. Historically a supplier to cable-television networks, the company has pivoted sharply toward hyperscale AI infrastructure. **Q1 2026 revenue reached $151.1 million**, up 51% from the year-earlier period, with data-centre sales representing 154% year-on-year growth and now accounting for 54% of the total. Management guides full-year 2026 revenue above $1 billion — more than double 2025's roughly $456 million — on the back of *800G* ramp volumes and a disclosed *1.6T* order worth over $200 million. The stock has gained roughly 496% over the past six months, closing in on an all-time high near $192 in early May 2026.

The bull thesis hinges on a claim about Nvidia's (NVDA) Blackwell architecture: that it is 30–50× more performant than the H100, with the corollary that its prodigious compute demands physically require *photonic* or optical connections. **The 30× figure is Nvidia's own marketing language**, but it compares a 72-GPU GB200 NVL72 rack-scale system — 72 Blackwell chips, 36 Grace CPUs, liquid-cooled — against H100-era multi-node clusters running trillion-parameter inference, not chip against chip. Standardised *MLPerf* benchmarks, which test individual chips on consistent workloads, show a single B200 achieving roughly 2–5× the throughput of an H100 depending on precision and task type. The gap is real and meaningful; the headline multiplier is a product of cherry-picked system comparisons.

The optical interconnect thesis is more defensible than the benchmark framing suggests. Inside a single rack, copper still dominates — Nvidia's NVL72 uses a passive copper backplane for its *NVLink* 6 internal network. But across racks and across the data-centre floor, *pluggable optical transceivers* at 400G and 800G are already the industry standard. The next evolution is *co-packaged optics* (CPO), which mounts the optical engine directly on the same substrate as the network switch chip, millimetres rather than centimetres away. This cuts power consumption roughly 3.5× per port (from about 16W to 4W per 800G interface) and reduces signal loss from roughly 22 dB to 4 dB. Nvidia has publicly committed to CPO-based *InfiniBand* and Ethernet products entering commercial production in 2026, with its Feynman-generation accelerator targeting a full CPO deployment. The physics argument is real; the transition is a matter of degree and timeline.

The risk for AAOI's bull case lies in market position. Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI) is not the volume leader in 800G data-centre transceivers — that role belongs to Coherent (COHR) and China-based InnoLight, with Lumentum (LITE) close behind. Coherent, whose market capitalisation is roughly forty times AAOI's and which signed a multi-year strategic agreement with Nvidia (NVDA) in early 2025, holds a structural manufacturing advantage: it fabricates on 6-inch *indium-phosphide* wafers, yielding four times as many chips per wafer as AAOI's 3-inch process. Analyst consensus on AAOI sits around $83 per share, well below the $400 target in the post, though the range is wide — from $25 at one extreme to $220 from Rosenblatt after the Q1 2026 print. The optical-in-AI thesis may prove right; whether AAOI is its primary beneficiary is the harder question.

concepts.definition: A module that converts electrical signals from a network switch or server into pulses of light for transmission over fibre-optic cable, and back again on receipt. In data centres, these are the workhorse links connecting servers across switching fabrics at speeds ranging from 100G to 1.6T (terabits per second). They are typically hot-swappable: a failed unit can be replaced in minutes without taking down the switch.

An approach in which the optical engine — the photonic chiplets that generate, modulate, and detect light — is mounted on the same substrate as the switching chip, millimetres away rather than centimetres. This cuts power consumption per port roughly 3–4× compared with pluggable modules and reduces signal loss dramatically, at the cost of repairability: a failed optical unit requires replacing the entire switch rather than just a module.

A removable optical module — typically in a QSFP-DD or OSFP form factor — that slides into a cage on a switch or server faceplate. Its key advantage is field-replaceability: a failed unit can be swapped in minutes. At 800G speeds and above, pluggable transceivers consume roughly 16W each, which is driving industry interest in co-packaged alternatives.

A data-rate standard for optical transceivers running at 800 gigabits per second, typically achieved by combining eight 100G lanes. Dominant in new hyperscale AI data-centre deployments as of 2025–2026. The next tier, 1.6T (1.6 terabits per second), began commercial deployment in 2025.

The next-generation optical interface standard after 800G, running at 1.6 terabits per second. Early commercial deployments began in 2025–2026, primarily for hyperscale AI clusters requiring extreme bandwidth density between top-of-rack switches.

A high-speed, low-latency network fabric standard widely used in high-performance computing and AI training clusters. Nvidia acquired InfiniBand leader Mellanox in 2020 and brands its AI-cluster networking products as Quantum (InfiniBand) and Spectrum (Ethernet). InfiniBand's tight latency guarantees make it preferred for GPU-to-GPU collective communication during model training.

An industry benchmark suite managed by MLCommons that measures AI hardware performance on standardised training and inference tasks. Unlike vendor-supplied figures, MLPerf results use consistent, reproducible workloads submitted under third-party audit, making them a useful corrective to marketing performance claims.

Nvidia's proprietary high-bandwidth chip-to-chip interconnect, used to connect multiple GPUs within a single server or rack at speeds far higher than PCIe. NVLink 6, used in the GB200 NVL72 rack system, connects 72 Blackwell GPUs via a passive copper backplane at aggregate bandwidths of hundreds of terabytes per second — without requiring any optical interconnect inside the rack.

A compound semiconductor material whose optical and electronic properties make it well-suited for fabricating the lasers and photodetectors used in high-speed optical transceivers. Larger wafer sizes — 6-inch versus the older 3-inch standard — yield more chips per fabrication run, a key cost and scaling advantage in high-volume transceiver manufacturing.

Relating to the generation, manipulation, and detection of photons (light particles) in semiconductor devices. Photonic integrated circuits combine lasers, modulators, and photodetectors on a single chip, enabling the compact, power-efficient optical engines used in co-packaged optics and high-speed transceivers.

article.fact_check: The claim that Nvidia Blackwell is 30–50× more performant than the H100 is misleading as stated. Nvidia's own 30× figure compares the GB200 NVL72 — a 72-GPU liquid-cooled rack system — against H100-era multi-node clusters running trillion-parameter LLM inference, not chip against chip. Standardised MLPerf benchmarks show a single B200 achieving roughly 2–5× the throughput of an H100 depending on workload and precision level. The performance gain is real and significant; the headline multiplier conflates system-level and chip-level comparisons. Separately, the Q1 figures cited in the post — revenue of $151.1M, data-centre revenue of $81.4M — are from Q1 2026 (reported May 7, 2026), not Q1 2025; the post does not specify a year but the numbers themselves are accurate.

ticker_aaoi.name: Applied Optoelectronics, Inc.
ticker_aaoi.blurb: Applied Optoelectronics is a Texas-based maker of optical components and transceivers, historically known for serving cable-television networks and a handful of hyperscale customers in cycles of feast and famine. The AI build-out has dragged it firmly into the data-centre supply chain, where it now competes for 400G, 800G, and 1.6T transceiver volumes against Lumentum, Coherent, Innolight, and Eoptolink.
ticker_aaoi.recent: Management is guiding to full-year 2026 revenue exceeding $1 billion, more than double 2025's roughly $456 million, on the back of 800G ramps and a single 1.6T order disclosed at over $200 million. The company aims to scale from roughly 90,000 800G units per month at end-2025 toward 500,000 800G/1.6T units per month by end-2026. The stock hit an all-time high near $192 in early May 2026, having traded as low as $12.56 within the last 52 weeks.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_cohr.name: Coherent Corp.
ticker_cohr.blurb: Coherent Corp. (formerly II-VI Incorporated, rebranded after the 2022 acquisition of Lumentum rival Coherent) develops and manufactures engineered materials, optoelectronic components, and laser systems across three segments: Networking, Materials, and Lasers. Its Networking segment — the primary AI data-center play — supplies indium-phosphide chips, transceiver modules, and silicon-photonics sub-assemblies to hyperscalers and networking OEMs. With roughly $5.8 billion in fiscal 2025 revenue, it is one of the largest vertically integrated photonics companies in the world.
ticker_cohr.recent: Coherent joined the S&P 500 in March 2026, the same month it announced general availability of the industry's first dual-laser QSFP28-DCO module — a compact form factor enabling 100G coherent transmission over a single fiber with up to 300 km reach. At OFC 2026 the company showcased an expanded InP portfolio including 400 mW CW lasers, 200G/400G photodiodes, and 800G/1.6T modulators. Fifteen analysts hold an average "Strong Buy" rating with a consensus 12-month price target near $278.

ticker_lite.name: Lumentum Holdings Inc.
ticker_lite.blurb: Lumentum makes the lasers, optical chips, and components that go into the high-speed transceivers wiring AI data centres together. Spun out of JDSU in 2015, it spent its first decade as a 3D-sensing and telecom-optics supplier of moderate growth. The AI-cluster build-out has remade it into one of the principal upstream beneficiaries of hyperscaler capex, alongside Coherent Corp.
ticker_lite.recent: Q1 fiscal-2026 set record revenue, with management citing AI-driven demand and an order book that runs into 2027. In March 2026 Nvidia announced a roughly $2 billion strategic investment paired with multi-year purchase commitments for co-packaged-optics components. The company joined the S&P 500 in March 2026; shares have surged on AI demand, leaving the stock at a forward P/E in the 60s, materially above peers.
